cf.title: Use Boyer-Moore-Horspool for simple LIKE contains patterns

input.subject: [PATCH] Use Boyer-Moore-Horspool for simple LIKE contains patterns

verdict_reasoning: The decisive objection is maintenance-fit-1. Message #13 measures a steady 2.7x slowdown on 4-symbol data, message #12 claims no bound, and affected users have no way to opt out. The list has to agree whether that trade is acceptable before code review makes sense. demand-1 adds that all evidence is synthetic and that v5 limits the gain to Const patterns. The goal itself drew no objection.

brief.title: Boyer-Moore-Horspool fast path for LIKE '%literal%' patterns
brief.problem: col LIKE '%literal%' is a common query shape, and the existing matcher tries each input position in turn, which is O(text * pattern) in the worst case. The author wants faster contains-searches for users who run such queries with medium or long literals.
brief.proposed_design: textlike and namelike check the pattern on the first call and cache either a BMH search state or a generic marker in FmgrInfo.fn_extra. As of v5/v6, only Const patterns use BMH, with a single literal between leading and trailing %, deterministic collation, and single-byte or UTF-8 encoding. The search checks the candidate's last byte, then compares the rest left to right.
author_claims: Constant-pattern contains-searches are about 19% to 57% faster in the v1 benchmark, with the gain growing with literal length.
Patterns that do not qualify cost at most about 1% more in wall-clock time.
Planner behavior and index-path choice, including pg_trgm, do not change.
v5 still has narrow regressions, up to about 1.8x on repetitive LATIN1 input; the author does not claim a no-regression bound.
The existing SB_MatchText, UTF8_MatchText and MB_MatchText code stays unchanged.
brief.thread_state: Greg Sabino Mullane and Haibo Yan reviewed several versions, and Bryan Green found a stale-pattern bug with PL/pgSQL variables, fixed in v3. Haibo Yan called v5 ready for community review, and v6 addresses his minor points, but no committer has replied.
unclear: No benchmarks on x86-64 at SQL level for v5/v6; the thread shows only AArch64 numbers.
v5 removed BMH for Params and prepared-statement parameters, but the thread gives no numbers on how much of the benefit this loses.
The thread does not say whether the remaining 2.7x regression on low-alphabet data is acceptable to committers.
The author does not say whether ILIKE or NOT LIKE support is planned.
The thread does not answer the earlier BMH/LIKE threads that Haibo Yan linked, including Tom Lane's message.

objections.title: Low-alphabet data gets slower after upgrade, with no way to opt out
objections.failure_scenario: A site stores DNA sequences or other 4-symbol strings in a text column and runs col LIKE '%<64-byte literal>%'. After a major-version upgrade the same scans run about 2.7 times slower. Nothing in EXPLAIN shows the change, and no setting turns it off.
objections.argument: In message #13, v5 still reaches a steady 2.7x regression on a 4-symbol alphabet at large input sizes. Message #12 reports up to 1.8x on repetitive LATIN1 data, and the author claims no bound. Message #11 shows that each fallback trades one regression class for another. The thresholds behind these numbers (6 bytes for single-byte, 4 for UTF-8) come from AArch64 SQL runs only. A committer would likely ask who decided this trade is acceptable for users who never asked for the change.
objections.author_must_show: What do x86-64 SQL-level numbers show for v6 on low-alphabet data, and how would an affected user get the old behaviour back?

critic.reasoning: Message #13 measures a steady 2.7x regression on a 4-symbol alphabet, and message #12 claims no bound. The thread shows no SQL-level x86-64 numbers for v5/v6, and nobody has decided whether the regression is acceptable.

objections.title: Const-only restriction may leave out most real contains-search queries
objections.failure_scenario: An application sends `where name like $1` through JDBC, an ORM or PL/pgSQL with the search term bound as a parameter. Since v5, that pattern takes the existing matcher on the first call and never uses BMH. The user upgrades, sees no speedup, and still carries the low-alphabet regression risk wherever literals are inlined.
objections.argument: Message #12 limits BMH to Const patterns, after message #4 found stale-pattern bugs with Params, so the parameterized case no longer benefits. All demand evidence is synthetic: generated 1M-row tables and pg_attribute loops (message #1), plus matcher matrices (messages #5, #9, #13), with no field report or user request. Users with slow contains-searches on large tables can already use a pg_trgm index, which this patch does not change. The thread gives no numbers on how much of the stated benefit survives the Const-only rule.
objections.author_must_show: Which real workloads send `LIKE '%literal%'` with a literal Const of at least 4 or 6 bytes over sequential scans, and how much time do they spend in the matcher?

critic.reasoning: All evidence in the thread is synthetic, and no message reports a real workload. v5 removed BMH for Params, and the thread gives no numbers on how much of the benefit that loses.

refuted.title: Earlier BMH/LIKE concerns linked in message #5 are never answered
refuted.failure_scenario: A user stores low-alphabet data such as DNA sequences or hex digests and runs col LIKE '%<64-byte constant>%'. After upgrading, the scan runs about 2.7 times slower, and no setting turns the fast path off. The user finds out from slower queries in production.
refuted.argument: Message #5 says the low-entropy regression "seems related to the concerns raised in the earlier BMH/LIKE discussions" and links them, including one by Tom Lane. No later message says what those discussions decided or why v5/v6 now meets their bar. Message #13 measures a stable 2.7x regression on a 4-symbol alphabet, and message #12 says the patch claims no no-regression bound. A committer would likely want that earlier objection answered on the record before taking on a known regression in a core operator.
refuted.author_must_show: What did the earlier BMH/LIKE discussions linked in message #5 object to, and why is a 2.7x regression on low-alphabet data now acceptable?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which states the same 2.7x low-alphabet regression with the same failure scenario. The material does not show what the linked earlier discussions say, so they cannot support a separate objection.

refuted.title: Second Boyer-Moore-Horspool implementation in utils/adt
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch fixes or tunes the BMH search in varlena.c, for example its skip-table sizing or a bounds case. The copy in like_bmh.c keeps the old logic, and no test fails to show that the two have drifted apart.
refuted.argument: Message #2 points out that varlena.c already has a BMH search. Message #3 keeps the code separate because of LIKE escape handling and caching in fn_extra. That explains why the setup differs, but not why the inner search loop is separate. Since v5, the LIKE copy also differs in its comparison order and in preloading the guard shift. So two search loops, tuned in different ways, now need separate maintenance.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the search loop be shared with varlena.c, with only the pattern extraction and caching kept specific to LIKE?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 raised this and saw no advantage in refactoring; message #3 gave the reasons and added a cross-reference comment. Since v5 the LIKE loop differs by design (guard byte first, left-to-right compare, preloaded shift), so a varlena.c fix would not carry over unchanged.

refuted.title: Every textlike call pays for dispatch; only literal Const patterns gain
refuted.failure_scenario: An application sends LIKE patterns as bound parameters and runs on generic plans, or calls LIKE from PL/pgSQL. It gets no speedup, and its LIKE calls still go through the new eligibility check and fn_extra dispatch. Ten such per-operator fast paths would add up in the same way.
refuted.argument: Since v5, only direct Const patterns use BMH, as message #12 says. Params, PL/pgSQL variables, LIKE ANY/ALL, ILIKE and NOT LIKE stay on the generic path. The only fallback-overhead numbers (about 1%) are from v1 in message #1, which used a different dispatch design. The thread does not measure how much of the original gain remains once Params are excluded.
refuted.author_must_show: What share of real-world contains-searches use literal constants, and what is the measured fallback overhead of v6 on the generic path?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 measures the fallback cost at about 1% or less, and message #3 shows +0.3% for v2. v5 caches the generic marker on the first call, as v1 did, with no per-row revalidation. The share-of-constants question is a duplicate of demand-1.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds like_bmh.c with measured length thresholds and a second BMH search loop beside the one in varlena.c.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: textlike and namelike gain a dispatch step on every call, and BMH is slower on low-alphabet and repetitive input.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: see objection demand-1: Const-only restriction may leave out most real contains-search queries

questions: What do SQL-level x86-64 benchmarks of v6 show for low-alphabet and repetitive input, compared with the existing matcher?
What is the worst-case slowdown of v6 against the existing matcher, and which inputs produce it?
How would a user whose data hits the 2.7x regression get the old matcher back?
Which real workloads run LIKE '%literal%' with a Const literal of at least 4 or 6 bytes over sequential scans, and how much time do they spend in the matcher?
What did the earlier BMH/LIKE threads linked in message #5 conclude, and how does v6 answer them?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the LIKE matcher in utils/adt and its encoding and collation rules. No committer has replied in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for byte-level match correctness across encodings and collations, and for every later report of a slower contains-search, with thresholds tuned on AArch64 only.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered the first review within three days and posted six versions, each addressing reviewer findings.

priority.reason: The query shape is common and reviewers engaged, but v5 still shows a 2.7x regression with no stated bound and no opt-out. The patch is about 23 KiB within utils/adt, but judging it needs benchmarks across encodings and architectures.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the escape handling, UTF-8 byte-boundary safety and the fn_extra caching rules were not checked. Only 3 of 14 messages were shown in full; the later numbers rest on the objections' citations.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: pgbench: faster version of tpcb-like transaction
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a built-in pgbench script, tpcb-func, that packs five of the seven tpcb-like commands into one PL/pgSQL function created during -i. This cuts client-server round trips, and the author reported about 2 to 3 times higher TPS when data is in memory and commits are fast.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch was marked Waiting for author during the commitfest and was returned with feedback because no updated version was posted. Fabien COELHO's review asked for changes: rename it, since pgbench does not implement TPC-B per spec, rename the function, fix style and add regression tests. Michael Paquier said release comparisons need the same set of tests and suggested documenting such scripts instead of adding them to the code.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch has been Waiting for author during the commitfest without updates,
moving to Returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow LISTEN on patterns
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Aleksander Alekseev, Trey Boudreau
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets LISTEN take a quoted LIKE pattern, such as `LISTEN 'c%'`, so that one session receives notifications on every matching channel. The author asked whether explicit syntax like LISTEN LIKE or LISTEN SIMILAR should mark pattern listens, and later sketched LIKE, ILIKE and SIMILAR TO variants with pattern-aware UNLISTEN.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it after two days. The thread does not say why, but it shows two open problems. Tom Lane said that earlier proposals had stalled on how LISTEN and UNLISTEN patterns interact, and that overlapping patterns could force N pattern matches per incoming notification. Telling whether one pattern covers another may work for simple LIKE patterns but almost certainly not for regexes, and the author agreed his design was superficial and needed rework.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It seems like a series of N such
commands could leave us in a state where we have to do N
pattern-matches to decide if a channel name is being listened
to, which seems annoyingly expensive.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support SK_SEARCHNULL / SK_SEARCHNOTNULL for heap-only scans
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes heap scans honor SK_SEARCHNULL and SK_SEARCHNOTNULL scan keys in HeapKeyTest(), which skey.h documents as supported only for index scans. The goal was convenience for extensions that scan tables directly without SPI; a later follow-up by Jacob Champion added planner pushdown of IS [NOT] NULL quals into Seq Scan as scan keys.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas saw no benefit in heapam support alone and asked that nodeSeqScan.c use it, with performance results, and that the table AM API get an 'amsearchnulls' field. The author wanted to defer the executor part to a later patch, so Heikki marked the entry Returned with Feedback. The later executor and planner patches got no visible review before the entry closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Ok, I don't think this patch on its own is a good idea, without the
other parts, so I'll mark this as Returned with Feedback in the commitfest.

precedents_retrieved.title: Make deparsing of column defaults faster
precedents_retrieved.summary: Jeff Janes proposed passing zero instead of the relation OID as the second argument to pg_get_expr when deparsing column defaults (in pg_dump, psql and other callers), on the grounds that defaults cannot contain Vars, which avoids building a deparse context and made pg_dump -s on a 1600-column table about 40 times faster. Peter Eisentraut offered an alternative patch that caches the deparse context in fn_extra of pg_get_expr across calls.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut noted that his in-progress generated columns patch would remove the assumption that defaults contain no Vars, and later that more work was needed to cover dumping and restoring tables with many columns, in particular the pg_restore slowness (deparse_context_for called from StoreAttrDefault) and check constraints. The author said he would pursue a different approach, a hash table for making column names unique, in a future commitfest, and asked for the entry to be closed. Peter Eisentraut marked it returned with feedback until a more complete solution exists.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm going to set this thread as returned with feedback until we have a
more complete solution.

precedents_retrieved.title: Faster pglz compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch speeds up pglz compression by about 1.4 times. It replaces macros with functions, uses a compact uint16-indexed hash table without prev pointers, and compares 4 bytes at a time during match search.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The last version (v9) failed on cfbot with an AddressSanitizer heap-buffer-overflow in pglz_hist_add, and Tomas Vondra reproduced the invalid read with valgrind. Andres Freund also found the single large patch hard to review relative to its benefit, and Tomas Vondra agreed it should be split into smaller parts. The entry went to waiting on author; the author planned one more refactoring attempt, and the visible messages do not show anything after that.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Independent of this failure, I'm worried about the cost/benefit analysis of a
pglz change that changes this much at once. It's quite hard to review.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add a greedy join search algorithm to handle large join problems
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds GOO (Greedy Operator Ordering), a greedy join search that repeatedly merges the legal join pair with the lowest estimated cost until one join remains. It is meant to replace GEQO for large join problems, enabled by `enable_goo_join_search` above geqo_threshold.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. On the withdrawal date the author posted v5 with plans for broader plan-quality tests and a hybrid greedy/DP approach. Tomas Vondra had said earlier that picking locally optimal joins is a flaw built into any greedy method.

precedents_retrieved.title: change regexp_substr first argument make tests more easier to understand
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the input string in the regexp_substr() regression tests in strings.sql from 'abcabcabc' to 'abcaXcaYc', so each match returns a different substring. A later version also changed the regexp_instr() tests the same way.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that these tests exist to show the functions' behavior with several copies of the target substring. With distinct substrings, a correct result could also come from the pattern failing to match elsewhere, so the change weakens the tests. Tomas Vondra had earlier asked whether the change made the tests weaker. The entry was then withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Thus, what Jian is proposing breaks the
tests: it's no longer perfectly clear whether the result is because
the function did what we expect, or because the pattern failed to
match anywhere else.

precedents_retrieved.title: Skip replicating the tables specified in except table option
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an EXCEPT TABLE clause to CREATE/ALTER PUBLICATION ... FOR ALL TABLES, which records excluded tables in pg_publication_rel and makes pgoutput skip their changes. A companion patch adds ALTER PUBLICATION ... RESET, which returns a publication to its default state before ALL TABLES with an exception list is added.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch after the thread went quiet. From mid-2022 the messages are rebases and commitfest reminders, and the author said he saw little interest from others. Earlier, Peter Eisentraut doubted the feature was worth the trouble and pointed to the cost of tracking negative dependencies. Peter Smith found the meaning of ALTER PUBLICATION combined with EXCEPT ambiguous, but these points did not decide the outcome.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As I did not see much interest from others, I'm withdrawing this patch
for now.

roaster_notes.note: The precedent index returned no matching attempt. Message #5 links earlier BMH/LIKE discussions, but the material does not report their content, so no prior attempt entry is listed.

The proposal adds no syntax, keyword, GUC, catalog object, psql feature or dump state, so nothing needs a pg_dump round-trip. Results stay the same as the existing matcher: nondeterministic collations and non-UTF-8 multibyte encodings keep the old path, and differential tests matched before and after the patch. The remaining issues are performance and design, which other angles cover.

The proposal changes no persistent or cross-node state: no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire message or existing struct changes. The BMH state lives only in per-backend FmgrInfo.fn_extra memory and LIKE results do not change, so standbys, subscribers and pg_upgrade are unaffected.

The patch changes only how textlike and namelike match a constant pattern, so it adds no privilege, role, GUC, catalog entry or new exposure. Bryan Green audited it for security (message #4), and the stale-pattern bug he found was a correctness issue, fixed in v3. The remaining slowdown is a constant factor of about 2.7x, linear in input size (message #13), so it does not give an unprivileged user a new denial-of-service path. Leakproofness and RLS behaviour are unchanged because the functions and the planner are the same.

Not applicable. Message #5 links earlier BMH/LIKE threads that the material does not include, so they could not be weighed. No committer has engaged in the visible thread, which bears on committability only.

Postgres already has two ways around slow '%literal%' searches. strpos() uses the BMH search in varlena.c, but every LIKE query, including generated ones, would have to be rewritten. A pg_trgm index avoids most scans but still rechecks rows with the LIKE matcher. Neither covers what the patch speeds up, and the thread settled the duplicate BMH code in messages #2 and #3.
The query shape is common and three reviewers engaged, but the material shows no user asking for this. The Const-only rule in v5 may shrink the group that benefits.
